titulo.texto: The Martyrs of Japan I: The Discovery

frase_gancho.texto: A mural some thirty meters long that lay under whitewash for generations, and whose painter no one remembers.

puente_narrativo.texto: Follow your route: it may lead you to read the mural at a calmer pace, or to the Museum of Sacred Art.

guion_corto.texto: Someone was cleaning the walls of the cathedral when a fish appeared. That is what some versions of the discovery of this mural say, a mural that had been covered with whitewash for generations. Beneath the layers of paint lay an enormous scene, about thirty meters long and eight meters high, about the martyrs of Nagasaki and Saint Philip of Jesus. It came to light during a major renovation ordered by Bishop Sergio Méndez Arceo, in the late 1950s. No one knows who painted it: it is attributed to an anonymous artist of the seventeenth or early eighteenth century. It tells a real episode, which took place in Japan in 1597 and which had a great echo in Mexico.

guion_largo.texto:
The story begins in Japan. On January eighteenth, 1597, the ruler Taicosama issued a sentence in Osaka. That is the name by which Spanish texts call Toyotomi Hideyoshi. The order: twenty-four Christians were to be crucified in Nagasaki. In the end there were twenty-six, among them Franciscans, Jesuits and laypeople. They were executed on February fifth of that year. One of them was Philip of Jesus, a young Franciscan born in Mexico City, and that is why his story mattered so much here. He is the first saint born in Mexico, and he was canonized in 1862.

One of the open questions is why this scene ended up painted in a convent in Cuernavaca. One hypothesis mentions Franciscans who passed through this convent on their way to martyrdom, such as Pedro Bautista, Martín de la Ascensión, Francisco Blanco and Francisco de San Miguel. Another links the painting to the wreck of the galleon San Francisco in 1609, off the coast of Japan. On that occasion more than three hundred sailors from New Spain were rescued. Neither of the two has been proven.

The mural measures about thirty meters long and eight meters high. It covers the walls of the nave, between the choir loft and the chancel arch, which is the great arch that separates the nave from the presbytery. Its author and its original title are unknown. Specialists date it between the middle of the seventeenth century and the early years of the next. Some link it to the period after 1628, when the beatification of Philip of Jesus was announced.

Then came the whitewash. During the modernization of the interiors, between the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, the walls were whitewashed and covered with neoclassical altarpieces. A researcher, María Elena Ota, links the whitewashing to the parish priest Vito Cruz Manjarrez, who held the post from 1867 to 1880.

The discovery has several versions. The renovation was ordered by Bishop Sergio Méndez Arceo and directed by Friar Gabriel Chávez de la Mora and the architect Ricardo de Robina. According to one author, the discovery was accidental. According to another, the Department of Colonial Monuments ordered the whitewash removed in order to look for paintings. A third says that fish could already be seen above the north door and that beneath them there were thirteen layers of paint. And a fourth says that a worker uncovered it while cleaning the walls left bare after the altars were removed. The sources give 1957 as the year of the discovery and 1959 for the restoration.

In that restoration the color was reintegrated, mostly ochres and blues. The repainting was criticized, because it was done without authorization and with colors that were too intense. They were softened afterward.

Precisely for that reason, it is worth looking carefully. What you see is an old painting, but also the result of a twentieth-century restoration.

texto: Look along the wall for the edge of the mural and try to imagine the nave covered in white whitewash
Think about the four versions of the discovery and decide which one seems most believable to you
Look for the ochre and blue colors that were repainted in the 1959 restoration

texto.pregunta: Myth: A Japanese artist painted the mural in Cuernavaca.
texto.respuesta: Reality: No one knows who painted it. Its style resembles East Asian art, but no one has proven that its author was Japanese.
